implement: legion-worker: the implementer opens the pull request, writes the body from the template, pushes its own commits and records a proof per acceptance line; this change spans eight packages and three documents, so the push, PR-body and proof rules decide whether the phase can complete at all.

legion-worker/references/pr-body.md: every proof here is a run of two real envoy-dispatch processes (or the CI run id of the new dispatch-multiprocess job), and this reference is the only definition of what counts as a proof and of the CI line.

legion-worker/references/conflicts-and-rewrites.md: the change touches docs/, api/, delivery/, outbox/ and cmd/dispatch/main.go, all busy files, so a conflict with main during the branch's life is likely and must be a forward merge rather than a rebase.
ce-simplify-code: step 8 of the plan is an explicit simplify pass over the whole change, and this skill defines it.
dispatch: the implementer posts no spec edit, but its production check and any blocker go through dispatch comment, dispatch message or dispatch ask, each with its own shape rules.
test: legion-worker: the tester drives the changed surface for real rather than re-running CI, judges whether the implementer's tests would catch what it broke, and records its own proof array; the whole verdict of this issue is a behavioural one (two processes, one database, one bus).

legion-worker/references/pr-body.md: it defines the tester's E2E line, its proof entries and the rule that lint, types and unit suites are CI's work, which matters here because the two-process test is slow and tempting to re-run by hand.
dispatch: a failure the tester reports to the architect, or a human to-do it finds (the DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY precondition is one), goes through the dispatch command and follows its shape rules.
review: legion-worker: the reviewer's round order (read the code commit's checks, push the handoff, review the head that push made, then complete) and its approval are what the merge gate reads.
legion-worker/references/merge-gate.md: this issue ends in a READY whose head INFRA-63 waits on, so the reviewer must know exactly what it approves and what retro may add above it.
legion-worker/references/review-threads.md: the review will be large (eight packages plus documentation), so threads are answered and resolved one by one rather than in bulk.
dispatch: the reviewer reads the issue's spec and plan.md beside the diff, and anything it must raise with the architect goes through the dispatch command.

findings.finding: F1: the two delivery durables cannot be reshaped in place (NATS permits only filter, AckWait and MaxAckPending to change), and during a rolling update the old build keeps reconciling the same durable name against the new one every 30 s. delivery-jobs is DeliverNewPolicy with no ack-floor-preserving recreation path, so a delete-and-recreate drops what arrives in the gap.
findings.answer: Plan section 1.1 and 2: the durables keep their names, shapes and policies. Nothing is deleted or recreated. The losing process becomes a standby that polls every 2 s and never gives up, the reconciliation runs only under the new duty lease, and its destructive branch is skipped entirely when ConsumerInfo reports the consumer PushBound.

findings.finding: F2: 'every background loop running once overall rather than once per process' is false as written. The SSE relay and the delivery live hub must run in every process or acceptance 2 fails, and migration 0107's own comment says the hub is per task by design.
findings.answer: Plan section 6.2 replaces the blanket criterion with a per-loop table of three classes (leased, already claimed, per-process by design) with a reason per row, and section 6.3 gives the machine-checkable form: each leased loop logs a run line and a skip line, and the two-process test counts them. Recorded as a departure; the architect owns the acceptance wording.

findings.finding: F3: 'each delivery and each outbox message handled exactly once' is unachievable across a crash, and the intake is at-most-once by design (delivery/intake.go acks every message whatever the handler did).
findings.answer: Plan sections 2 and 3 state the honest criterion per lane: a delivery is handled at most once from the bus and converged by the 5-minute reconcile; every events row reaches published_at once; each JetStream destination holds one retained message per dedupe key and topic in the 72 h window; core-transport role lanes are at-least-once with no bus suppression, which is written down rather than fixed. Recorded as a departure.

findings.finding: F4: 'proven by a test that fails against the code before this change' has no surface: nothing in the repository runs a Dispatch process with NATS enabled, and the reviewer needs a repeatable way to see the 'fails before' half.
findings.answer: Plan section 9.1 builds the surface: a //go:build multiprocess test in cmd/dispatch over storetest.Open plus testnats.Start, two real binaries on one database and one bus, with its own CI job modelled on dispatch-memory so go test's 10-minute package deadline is not the budget. Section 9.2 requires each row's failure at the base commit to be recorded as its exact go test -run invocation and output in the pull request body.

findings.finding: F5: the issue never says what the migration rule is, and three standing documents say the opposite (cmd/dispatch/README.md mandates Recreate for 0113, deploy/README.md asserts two releases never serve together, and the published running-dispatch page tells operators not to roll).
findings.answer: Plan section 8 states the rule (a migration must leave the release before it able to read and write the schema; expand then contract across two releases; a migration that cannot be written that way is a named exception, not a default) and lists the five places it lands, including rescoping the 0113 paragraph as that migration's own instruction rather than the standing rule, and a new README beside the migrations directory.

findings.finding: F6: acceptance 2's document half reads two ways, and under either reading the durable corruptions a second live room causes are not optional and the spec does not name them.
findings.answer: Plan section 5 splits it: 5.1 is the non-negotiable durable-correctness gate (a per-room applied cursor and a refusal to append, settle, version, fork-live or rebuild from a room whose cursor is not equal to the durable head), with the seven durable corruptions enumerated and cited; 5.2 is the notify-driven refresh; 5.3 is the statement acceptance 2 asks for and where it is written. Cross-process live co-editing is reported to the architect as a follow-up.

findings.finding: F7: two processes without DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY mint their own session signing keys in their own data directories, so every person is signed out by whichever replica answers next and every stored refresh token reads as absent. No health check sees it, and the issue does not mention identity.
findings.answer: Plan section 7: the server cannot detect it (one process cannot learn another's key), so DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY becomes a hard, written precondition of a multi-process deployment, the two-process test asserts a cookie minted on one process authenticates on the other with the negative control of differing keys, and it heads the precondition list section 10 hands to INFRA-63. No new setting and no key fingerprint on a public probe.

findings.finding: F8: the Dispatch deployment this issue serves is not in this repository; the only one here is a single compose container whose deployer stops the old one first, and whether the front door is session-sticky cannot be read from here.
findings.answer: Plan section 10 records it as an assumption carried from INFRA-62, not a measured fact, and makes the design independent of it: nothing in this plan depends on a reader staying on one process, so no stickiness is assumed. Plan section 8 scopes the compose deployment's 'never serve together' sentence to that deployment rather than deleting it.

findings.finding: F9: the SSE fix must preserve the handler's subscribe-before-head argument, and the in-process broker it would be taken off is also the outbox's wake.
findings.answer: Plan section 4 keeps events.Broker and every s.publish call site exactly as they are for the local wake, adds a separate events.Stream fed only by the relay, and restates the no-gap argument in full, including the one new live-loop drop (id <= since) that a lagging relay makes necessary and why it is not the comparison the handler's comment forbids. The outbox's cross-process wake is its existing 5 s ticker; the delivery hub already has its own listen.

findings.finding: F10: a lease has an advisory-lock key space to obey (the single-key space is shared with document rooms, rank allocation, agent artifacts, the commit order and the migration runner) and cannot live on a pooled connection that the pool may recycle.
findings.answer: Plan section 6.1: the lease uses the two-key form with a namespace of its own (0x4C4F4F50), as copied asks do, and adds a line to the enumeration in docs/copied_asks.go. It takes a session lock on a connection of its own from a new store.Pool.Leases(), built with the same separate machinery as Rooms and Listener, holds no transaction, and destroys the connection rather than returning it if the unlock fails.

findings.finding: F11: NATS grants for any new durable, subject or bucket cannot be verified from this repository, and Dispatch already meets publish denials in production.
findings.answer: Plan section 1: the design deliberately adds no NATS subject, durable, consumer or KV bucket, so no grant change is needed and no cross-repository prerequisite is created. Section 10 states that explicitly as a line INFRA-63 can rely on, and marks the grant itself as unread from here.

findings.finding: F12: /healthz reports nothing about the delivery durables or about which process holds a singleton, and the deploy check that reads its commit field stops being deterministic when two builds answer one address.
findings.answer: Plan section 10 decides explicitly that /healthz does not change, with the reason: a non-leader is not unhealthy, and a probe that failed on one would have the load balancer replace a working replica. How a roll is verified when two builds answer one address is handed to INFRA-63 as a named open item rather than left implicit.

findings.finding: F13: 'the handoff names the commit this merged as' cannot be satisfied by a handoff, because the merge commit does not exist when the last handoff is written and retro removes .legion/<issue>/ from the head that merges.
findings.answer: Plan section 10 names the artifact that can hold it: the architect's sign-off comment on this issue, written from the implementer's production check. Recorded as a departure and reported to the architect, since the acceptance wording is the architect's.

findings.finding: F14: 'until it merges, INFRA-63 may not raise the replica count' reads as a complete gate, but the signing key, the front door, the grant and the deploy verification are all outside this issue's merge.
findings.answer: Plan section 10 is that precondition list, written for the implementer's handoff and the architect to carry: the signing key, the unchanged grant, the deploy verification of a two-build roll, asset and API skew between builds, and the front door's stickiness being an assumption rather than a dependency.

findings.finding: F15: two of the spec's three named per-process loops are mis-stated. The settlement resumption is written for cross-process overlap, and the webhook sweeper is already multi-process-safe through NATS key-value compare-and-set; the loops that genuinely multiply a scarce resource are the two GitHub importers the spec does not name.
findings.answer: Plan section 6.2 corrects the list with citations, keeps the settlement resumption per-process by design, and leases the two GitHub importers and the sweeper for their rate-limit cost rather than for correctness. Recorded as a departure so the plan is not read as the spec's bullet list.

findings.finding: F16: a rolling update makes build skew user-visible beyond migrations (asset chunks served by the wrong build, API shape, no binary-versus-schema check at boot), and the spec scopes only migrations.
findings.answer: Plan section 10 draws the scope line explicitly: schema compatibility is this issue's (section 8), and asset and API skew between two live builds is the deployment's, with DISPATCH_ASSET_STORE_BUCKET named as the mechanism. Reported to the architect as a scope line rather than silently absorbed or dropped.

findings.finding: F17: four citations do not resolve as given, among them the planner's own e2e/run-server.sh path, which is under packages/dispatch and pins NATS off and a per-process dev signing key, so it cannot be the two-process surface for bus defects.
findings.answer: The plan re-anchors every citation to a construct read at the base commit, names packages/dispatch/e2e/run-server.sh correctly in section 9.1 and rules it out for exactly that reason, and the plan review spot-checked the twelve citations the design turns on and found each resolving to the construct named.

specDepartures.spec: Acceptance 1: 'every background loop running once overall rather than once per process.'
specDepartures.plan: A per-loop table decides one of three classes per loop: leased singleton, already claimed, or per-process by design. The reader stream relay, the delivery live hub and its listener, the document settlement resumption, the room timers and the HTTP server stay per-process.
specDepartures.evidence: The delivery live hub must run in every process or acceptance 2 fails: migration 0107_events_notify.up.sql's own comment says the trigger exists so that 'every committed event wakes each Dispatch task's delivery hub', and docs/resume.go:16-21 says the settlement resumption runs on an interval precisely because a rolling deploy overlaps two processes.

acceptance: Acceptance 1's loop clause becomes the plan's table, with the per-loop reason, and the machine-checkable form is a run/skip count per leased loop asserted by the two-process test.

specDepartures.spec: Acceptance 1: 'each delivery and each outbox message handled exactly once.'
specDepartures.plan: A criterion per lane: a GitHub delivery is handled at most once from the bus and converged by the five-minute reconcile; every events row reaches published_at exactly once; each JetStream destination holds one retained message per dedupe key and topic inside the 72-hour window; core-transport role lanes are at-least-once and say so.
specDepartures.evidence: delivery/intake.go:347-356 acks every message whatever the handler did, so the bus half is at most once by design, not exactly once. outbox/publisher.go:140-149 publishes then marks, so a crash between the two republishes. bus/nats.go:669-672 sends notifications.role.* over core NATS with no message id, so the stream suppresses nothing there at any replica count.

acceptance: Acceptance 1's 'exactly once' becomes the four per-lane criteria above, each with the assertion that decides it.

specDepartures.spec: Acceptance 4: 'the handoff names the commit this merged as, because INFRA-63 waits on it.'
specDepartures.plan: The architect's sign-off comment on this issue names the merge commit, written from the implementer's production check.
specDepartures.evidence: No handoff can carry it: the merge commit does not exist when the last handoff is written, and retro's final commit removes .legion/<issue>/ from the head that merges, so nothing under .legion survives onto the default branch.

acceptance: Acceptance 4 names the architect's sign-off comment on this issue as the artifact, rather than a handoff.

specDepartures.spec: What breaks today: 'Several background loops run once per process: the webhook sweeper, the delivery reconcile, the settlement resumption.'
specDepartures.plan: The settlement resumption stays per-process and is not changed. The webhook sweeper is already correct across processes and is leased only for its GitHub call cost. The loops that genuinely multiply a scarce resource are the delivery reconcile and the architecture import, the second of which the spec does not name.
specDepartures.evidence: docs/resume.go:16-21 describes the overlapping-deploy case the loop exists for. redeliver/sweep.go:693-704 claims each delivery by a key-value compare-and-set 'so two sweepers never both request one attempt'. architecture.Run is started beside the reconcile at cmd/dispatch/main.go:368 and makes the same per-installation GitHub calls.

summary: The 'what breaks today' list is corrected: the settlement resumption and the webhook sweeper are not broken at more than one process, and the architecture import belongs on the list.

specDepartures.spec: The bullet list of what breaks today, and acceptance 2's allowance that the design may say why a document open on one process does not see the other's writes as a live session.
specDepartures.plan: The plan takes that allowance for the live session, and adds work the spec's bullets do not name: a per-room applied cursor and a refusal to append, settle, version, fork-live or rebuild from a room whose cursor is not equal to the durable head, plus a notify-driven eviction of a stale room. It also adds the session signing key as a written precondition of a multi-process deployment.
specDepartures.evidence: A settlement reads its cursor from the database under the room's advisory lock (docs/service.go:1205,1224) but renders its version from its own process's room (docs/service.go:1140-1146,1247), then writes doc_update_version and clears doc_settlements_pending; so a second live room durably versions text it does not hold and retracts open asks whose blocks it cannot see (docs/ask_blocks.go:390-398,168-176). Without DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY each process mints its own key (cmd/dispatch/main.go:750-757), so cookies minted on one are refused by the other.

outcome.scope: Two items are added beyond the spec's bullets: the document durable-correctness gate, which is the largest and riskiest part of the change, and the signing-key precondition with its test. Cross-process live co-editing of one document is excluded and reported to the architect as a follow-up issue.
